pitch_detail.notes: From high camp below the glacier, rope up and cross the lower Boulder Glacier heading northwest to the toe of the Boulder–Park Cleaver, near 6,800 ft. A few crevasses and icefall bands lie on this crossing. Parties that instead climb the glacier's central section meet far more broken ground and unreliable, undercut bridges by midsummer.

Follow the cleaver, mostly on its north side, with a short rock scramble around 7,800 ft; this middle section is largely crevasse-free. Flat bivy sites along the rib (around 7,200–7,500 ft) allow a shorter summit day, and a flat spot near 8,800 ft is the place to study the upper mountain. Higher, the snow can be steep, icy and exposed to rockfall, with crevasses close below.

At the large rock buttress near 9,300 ft, head up toward its toe and traverse south toward Sherman Crater on moderate snow, weaving through crevasses; the pattern here dictates the line and is very broken by midsummer. The traverse passes beneath the buttress, so helmets and pace matter. From the crater side, finish up steep glacier between the vents and the summit plateau.

Alternative to the snow traverse: climb the rock buttress above 9,300 ft directly on 4th-class ground, or skirt its north edge on a short snow or ice slope, then angle onto Grant Peak. Cliffs drop steeply near the summit, and the whole face gets early sun, so start early to be off it before rockfall begins.

wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.beta: From a high camp below the Boulder Glacier (~5,500 ft), cross the lower Boulder Glacier northwest to the toe of the Boulder-Park Cleaver (~6,800 ft) and follow the cleaver up. Above about 9,300 ft, choose between a moderate 25-35° snow traverse toward Sherman Crater, or a harder 4th-class rock buttress direct to the summit area.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier.overview: A classic, less-crowded glacier route up the east side of Baker via the Boulder Glacier and Boulder Cleaver. It's the steepest of Baker's standard glacier routes but not technically difficult once above the approach — the real crux is the arduous, unmaintained approach trail, which keeps crowds well below the Coleman-Deming or Easton Glacier routes.

pitch_detail.notes: Boulder Ridge Trail #605, ~2 miles to wilderness boundary/bog
Steep heather and a short fixed-line rock step to ~5,700 ft camp
Cross glacier to base of cleaver (~6,800 ft), navigating crevasses
Steeper, icy, rockfall-exposed climbing with crevasses close below; ice screws and pickets for protection
Running belay with pickets and screws under a rock band

wa_eldorado_peak_northeast_face.beta: From the East Ridge glacier approach, at roughly 7,500-8,200 ft leave the standard track and angle up and right beneath a rock band on 50-60° snow/ice, protected with a running belay of pickets and ice screws, then join the summit knife-edge near the top of the East Ridge.

pitch_detail.notes: 60m of water ice, the technical crux.
Roughly four additional roped pitches on steepening ice and snowfields.
Rime-covered ridge and an icy chimney lead to the summit.

wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.beta: Technical ice and mixed climbing route on the northwest face. Begins at the Shooting Gallery route junction with a WI4 pitch immediately right of the prominent hanging glacier. Climbers then simul-climb along the western upper amphitheater basin (between Lincoln and Assassin Spire), followed by approximately four roped pitches on steeper ice with snowfields up to 70° in between, concluding with rime-covered ridge climbing to the summit. Route benefits from 'all-time conditions' with nearly snowless winter and solid ice formation. Descent typically via southwest face route.
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.overview: This slot corresponds to 'Wilkes-Booth,' a ~2,000-ft ice/mixed line on Lincoln Peak's NW Face — the only established route on the mountain besides the historic SW Face X Couloir. First climbed by Michal Rynkiewicz and Daniel Coltrane on March 13, 2015, in an 18.5-hour car-to-car push from the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead during a rare one-day weather window. The crux is the lower portion of the first pitch (60m, WI4), which shares its start with the 'Shooting Gallery' route on nearby Assassin Spire.
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.approach: Same trailhead and lower approach as the standard line: start at the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (FS Road 39, Trail #677) near Glacier, WA, and follow the Heliotrope Ridge Trail roughly 2 miles through old-growth forest and several avalanche-chute creek crossings to the flat former Kulshan Cabin site (~4,700 ft), the usual camp/staging area. From there, climb the Hogsback moraine to the toe of the Coleman Glacier and rope up for glacier travel — but where the standard route cuts southwest toward the Thunder Glacier cirque, the north ridge/north-face approach stays higher and further climber's-right (east) on the Coleman Glacier, traversing beneath the Coleman icefall to reach the north-facing cirque wedged between Colfax Peak and Lincoln Peak. This is a longer, more exposed glacier traverse than the standard approach: you pass directly beneath active serac bands on the Coleman Glacier's upper icefall for a stretch, so icefall/serac collapse is a real objective hazard here and timing (early morning, before the glacier softens) matters more than on the SW-side approach. The line aims for the base of Lincoln's northwest face, where the route climbs roughly 2,000 ft of steep ice and mixed ground — genuinely an ice/mixed objective, not a snow scramble, and conditions (rime, verglas, bare ice) vary a lot by season and year; go early-season (spring) for the best ice, which also generally means better-bridged crevasses on the glacier crossing.
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.descent_text: There is no walk-off from the top of the north ridge/north face — it's a rappelling descent back down steep, often loose terrain. Because the north face has no established independent descent line, parties either reverse the ridge/face itself or (more commonly, per the pattern typical of routes like this) traverse over on the upper mountain to descend the easier, well-traveled southwest gully (the 'X Couloir' used as the standard route's descent) rather than rappel the full north face a second time. Reversing the route means building rappel anchors off slung rock horns and blocks through the steepest ice and mixed sections — the rock here is loose, so test anchors and blocks carefully and avoid pulling ropes across bare rock edges. Given the line is roughly 2,000 ft (~610m) with steep ice sections separated by snowfields, and using a single rope doubled (~30m per rappel) is the standard setup for anchors of this type, expect on the order of 4-6 rappels through the steepest ice/mixed sections with some downclimbing or simul-climbing on the more moderate snow between them if descending the face directly; if instead you traverse to the standard SW gully, expect a rappel sequence similar to that route's (commonly up to 10 double-rope rappels off a mix of pickets and existing horn slings, conditions-dependent). Either way, re-rope once back on the Coleman Glacier for the crevassed descent back to the Hogsback moraine and the Heliotrope Ridge Trail.
